con-disco , dĭdĭci, 3, v. a. *
I. To learn with or in company with one: “ex his, qui mihi Athenis condidicere,” App. Flor. 3 , n. 18, p. 362, 8.—
II. To learn carefully, eagerly, or well, to learn thoroughly (rare but class. in prose and poetry).
(a). With acc.: “modos,” Hor. C. 4, 11, 34 : “crimen a teneris annis,” Ov. H. 4, 25 : genera plausuum, *Suet. Ner. 20: “pacem oculis,” Sil. 7, 462 .—Far more freq.,
(b). With inf.: “ego istuc aliis dare condidici,” Plaut. Ps. 4, 1, 34 : “merum bibere,” id. Curc. 1, 3, 4 ; 4, 3, 2; id. Poen. 3, 1, 11: “mihi paulo diligentius supplicare,” Cic. Planc. 5, 13 ; * Quint. 1, 9, 2: “foris pasci,” Col. 7, 3, 19 : “pauperiem pati,” Hor. C. 3, 2, 3 .—*
(g). With a relative-clause: “condiscere qui pecuniae fructus esset,” Cic. Quint. 3, 12 .—
B. Transf., of inanim. subjects: “ut (flagellum) paulatim condiscat suis radicibus ali,” Col. 4, 15, 3 ; so id. 3, 10, 16; Plin. 21, 5, 11, § 24.
From A Latin Dictionary (Charlton T. Lewis, Charles Short, Oxford, Clarendon Press, 1879)
